## Simple explanation

Ensemble learning combines multiple models so that their collective
prediction may be more accurate or robust than an individual model.
Common examples include random forests and boosting methods.

## Technical explanation

Ensembles combine model outputs through averaging, voting, weighted
combination, or sequential correction. Bagging trains models on
resampled data to reduce variance; boosting fits learners in sequence to
address errors; stacking trains a meta-model on base-model predictions.
Benefits depend on model quality and diversity.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Ensembles can improve performance or stability, especially when component
models make different errors. They also add inference cost, complexity,
and monitoring requirements.

## How it works

Train multiple models using different data samples, features,
initializations, or objectives. Combine their predictions with a
predefined rule or learned meta-model. Evaluate the full ensemble against
the same held-out data and operational constraints as individual models.

## Practical example

A random forest combines predictions from many decision trees trained
with varied samples and feature choices. Their aggregate can be less
sensitive to the quirks of one tree.

## Common misconceptions

- An ensemble is not guaranteed to outperform its best component model.
- Identical models making identical errors provide little ensemble
  benefit.
- Better benchmark performance may not justify increased latency or
  operational complexity.
